history_of_present_illness: Tsutsugamushi is an acute febrile disease caused by the bite of a larval Kedani mite. The onset is characterized by headache, giddiness, a rapidly rising temperature, and swelling of the lymphatic glands draining the region of a small necrotic ulcer marking the bite site. With injected conjunctivae, continuous fever, and hyperaesthesia, the disease progresses for about a week. A macular eruption then appears, starting on the face, spreading to the chest, extremities, and trunk. Approximately ten days after the eruption, the fever falls by lysis. About one week post-bite, patients experience chilliness, giddiness, and headache, with rising temperature. Within two to three days, painful glands are noticed in regions like the groin, axilla, or neck, leading to the small necrotic ulcer often found in the armpit or genital region. This ulcer has a dark red areola and is only slightly tender. Glands are not excessively enlarged or tender, though general glandular enlargement may occur. The body is notably hyperaesthetic, conjunctivae are injected, and deafness is frequent. The tongue becomes dry and cracked, and a cough is often present. The eruption, which never becomes petechial, disappears in 7 to 10 days, and the fever becomes remittent or intermittent before normalizing. Parotitis may occur as a complication. The initial temperature is 101° to 103°F, later becoming higher and continuous, reaching 104°F or 105°F.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The disease has been known for over 1000 years. Its geographical distribution is limited to the western part of Nippon island, specifically when the banks of the Shinanogawa are inundated each spring. While primarily confined to Japan, a possibly identical disease was observed in the Philippines. The disease is caused by the bite of the larval mite, *Trombidium akamushi (Leptotrombidium akamushi)*, a minute orange-red arachnoid. This mite is only a source of danger in the region of inundated river banks, with bites elsewhere not causing the disease. Persons harvesting hemp during August are particularly susceptible if bitten. Field mice serve as a reservoir for the mite, found in large numbers on their ears, though the mice themselves do not appear ill. The disease is not communicable from person to person. The causative agent, which is unknown but has been attributed to various bacteria, a protozoon, or a virus, is present in the blood (0.001 cc to 0.1 cc can infect a monkey) and enlarged lymph glands. The virus is destroyed by heating blood at 50°C for 10 minutes. Hayashi reported minute rod, ring-shaped or spheroid bodies, resembling bacteria and organisms of typhus and spotted fever, as the cause, found in lymphocytes, endothelial phagocytes of lymph nodes and spleen, and in severe cases, in red blood cells and blood plasma. He suggests the organism resembles *Theileria parva* and *Bartonella bacilliformis*.
vitals: Pulse rate: 80-100 bpm. Temperature: 101-103°F (initially), rising to 104°F or even 105°F.
physical_exam: A small necrotic ulcer, about ⅙ inch in diameter, with a dusky red areola, is noted at the site of the larval mite bite, healing slowly into convalescence. There is characteristic swelling of the glands proximal to this initial ulcer, with connecting lymphatics potentially inflamed. Later, other glands may show slight swelling and tenderness. The glands are generally not excessively enlarged or tender. The spleen is usually enlarged, and there may be swelling of the mesenteric glands. The lower part of the ileum may show injection. Conjunctivae are injected. The body exhibits marked hyperaesthesia. A dusky macular eruption appears about one week after onset, first on the face (cheeks), then spreading to the chest, legs, forearms, and trunk, but is not prominent on the neck, arms, or thighs. This eruption never becomes petechial. The tongue often appears dry and cracked.
labs_and_diagnostics: The blood shows a leucopenia, with no change in red cells. Nagayo reported finding piroplasm-like forms in the spleen and lymphatic glands. Kawamuro and colleagues were unable to demonstrate any organism through various examination methods. Hayashi reported minute rod, ring-shaped or spheroid bodies, stainable with Giemsa’s stain, in the lymphocytes and endothelial phagocytes of lymph nodes and spleen. These bodies also occur in the blood plasma and, in severe cases, in red blood cells. These bodies resemble bacteria, similar to organisms of typhus and spotted fever, and are regarded by Hayashi as resembling *Theileria parva* and *Bartonella bacilliformis*. The virus is present in the blood and enlarged lymph glands.
differential_diagnosis: Plague, Typhus fever (Tabardillo, Brill’s disease), Spotted fever of the Rocky Mountains.
management_and_clinical_course: There is no specific treatment for Tsutsugamushi. Drugs may be necessary to combat insomnia. The serum of monkeys that have recovered from the disease appears to have some therapeutic value. The mortality rate in Japan is reported to be 30%.
